primary.key: Foot-prints are made by the shoe: they are not the shoe itself.
primary.s: Lao Tzŭ tells Confucius, whose Six Canons no ruler adopted, that they are old tracks; Guo Xiang, on 14.132, reads the shoe as what is so of itself, and the Canons as the print of one who leaves each thing to its true nature.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 14, on 14.132, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 16, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6365115 (2026)

basis.words: 所以迹者，真性也。夫任物之真性者，其迹則《六經》也。…況今之人事，則以自然為履，《六經》為迹。
basis.gloss: What makes the tracks is the true nature: for one who leaves things to their true nature, his tracks are the Six Classics. … So in the affairs of people now, take what is so of itself as the shoe, and the Six Classics as the tracks.

standby.key: That woman saw the beauty of knitted brows, but she did not see wherein the beauty of knitted brows lay.
standby.s: Among Shih Chin’s likenesses for Confucius’ revival of old ways is a woman who aped a beauty’s frown; Guo Xiang, on 14.83, reads rites and duty used in their time as Hsi Shih, and kept past their time as the ugly woman.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 14, on 14.83, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 16, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6365115 (2026)

basis.words: 況夫禮義，當其時而用之，則西施也；時過而不棄，則醜人也。
basis.gloss: How much more so with rites and duty: used when it is their time, they are Xi Shi (Hsi Shih); kept and not cast off when their time has passed, they are the ugly woman.

primary.key: If the age was unsuitable and their mission at failure, they fell back upon their own resources and waited.
primary.s: The chapter denies that the retired scholars of old hid, blaming the times; Guo Xiang, on 16.27, reads the waiting as a sage’s calm in a busy age: rooted deep, he waits for things to act of themselves, so the Way is not lost.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 16, on 16.27, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 18, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6365330 (2026)

basis.words: 雖有事之世，而聖人未始不澹漠也，故深根寧極而待其自為耳，斯道之所以不喪也。
basis.gloss: Even in an age given to affairs, the sage is never other than calm and unmoved; so he roots himself deep, rests in the ultimate, and waits for things to act of themselves; this is how the Way is not lost.

standby.key: That which is adventitious, comes. Coming, you cannot prevent it; going, you cannot arrest it.
standby.s: Once attaining one’s wish meant full joy, the chapter says, but now it means office; Guo Xiang, on 16.30, reads office as an outward thing whose gain and loss are not the self, worn calmly by one unaware it is lodged on him.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 16, on 16.30, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 18, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 6365330 (2026)

basis.words: 在外物耳，得失之非我也。…淡然自若，不覺寄之在身。
basis.gloss: It lies only among outward things; gaining and losing it are not the self. … (On the next line, not indulging one’s will for office:) calm and at ease as ever, not aware that the lodged thing is on his person.

primary.key: In the universe I am but as a small stone or a small tree on a vast mountain.
primary.s: Praised by the humbled River, the Spirit of the Ocean declines to boast; Guo Xiang, on 17.10, reads the words as seeming to belittle the small beside the great, though their sense is that each thing, knowing its limit, rests in its portion.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 17, on 17.10, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 19, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907030 (2026)

basis.words: 此發辭氣者，有似乎觀大可以明小，尋其意則不然。…然後惑者有由而反，各知其極，物安其分，逍遙者用其本步而遊乎自得之場矣。
basis.gloss: The tone in which this is said seems as if looking at the great could show up the small; but seek its meaning and it is not so. … Then the deluded have a way back: each knows its own limit, things rest in their portion, and the free and easy use their own stride to roam in the field of their own content.

standby.key: He who clearly apprehends the scheme of existence, does not rejoice over life, nor repine at death; for he knows that terms are not final.
standby.s: After space, time and fortune, the Ocean’s Spirit turns to life and death; Guo Xiang, on 17.20, reads the terms as end and beginning renewed daily: the old cannot be held, so the new is met without alarm and death and life change as one.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 17, on 17.20, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 19, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907030 (2026)

basis.words: 明終始之日新也，則知故之不可執而留矣，是以涉日新而不愕，舍故而不驚，死生之化若一。
basis.gloss: Clear that ending and beginning are renewed day by day, he knows that the old cannot be grasped and kept; so he passes into the daily new without alarm and lets go the old without fright, and the change of death and life is as one.

primary.key: Your very question shows that you knew I knew.
primary.s: On the Hao bridge, Hui Tzŭ denies anyone but a fish can know its pleasure; Guo Xiang, on 17.149, reads it as saying no one need be a fish to know fishes, since Hui Tzŭ knew Chuang Tzŭ was no fish without being him.
primary.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 17, on 17.149, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 19, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907030 (2026)

basis.words: 今子非我也，而云汝安知魚樂者，是知我之非魚也。苟知我之非魚，則凡相知者，果可以此知彼，不待是魚然後知魚也。
basis.gloss: Now you are not I, yet in saying ‘how do you know the pleasure of fish’ you know that I am not a fish. If you know that I am not a fish, then all who know one another can indeed know that one from this one, and need not be a fish before they know the fish.

standby.key: “Therefore it has been said, do not let the artificial obliterate the natural; do not let will obliterate destiny; do not let virtue be sacrificed to fame. Diligently observe these precepts without fail, and thus you will revert to the divine.”
standby.s: Having named four feet natural and the halter artificial, the Spirit of the Ocean gives three rules; Guo Xiang, on 17.79, reads the first as allowing halter and nose-string but forbidding that the beasts be driven past their portion.
standby.src: Guo Xiang, Zhuangzi zhu, chapter 17, on 17.79, zh.wikisource (Nanhua zhenjing zhushu, juan 19, Zhengtong Daozang), revision 7907030 (2026)

basis.words: 穿落之可也，若乃走作過分，羅步失節，則天理滅矣。
basis.gloss: Piercing the nose and haltering the head are permissible; but if they are made to run beyond their portion and their gait loses its measure, then the heavenly principle is destroyed.
